claim: Attentional capture by an irrelevant salient distractor is attenuated when the distractor appears more frequently in one location.
source: Attentional capture by an irrelevant salient distractor is attenuated when the distractor appears more frequently in one location, suggesting learned suppression of that location.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding that motivates the study.

claim: It remains unclear whether suppression is proactive (before attention is directed) or reactive (after attention is allocated).
source: However, it remains unclear whether suppression is proactive (before attention is directed) or reactive (after attention is allocated).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as the research question in the abstract.

claim: Participants searched for a shape singleton while ignoring a color singleton distractor at a high-probability location in an EEG experiment.
source: In an EEG experiment, participants searched for a shape singleton while ignoring a color singleton distractor at a high-probability location.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Search was more efficient when the distractor appeared at the high-probability location.
source: Behaviorally, search was more efficient when the distractor appeared at the high-probability location.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the experiment reported in the abstract.

claim: Inverted encoding analysis of EEG data showed tuning profiles that decayed during memory maintenance but were revived by the placeholder display.
source: Inverted encoding analysis of EEG data showed tuning profiles that decayed during memory maintenance but were revived by the placeholder display.
evidence: This describes a key neural finding from the EEG analysis.

claim: Tuning was most pronounced at the to-be-suppressed location, suggesting initial spatial selection followed by suppression.
source: Notably, tuning was most pronounced at the to-be-suppressed location, suggesting initial spatial selection followed by suppression.
evidence: This is the main finding from the tuning profile analysis.

claim: Learned distractor suppression is a reactive process.
source: These findings suggest that learned distractor suppression is a reactive process, providing new insights into learned spatial distractor suppression mechanisms.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Visual input is highly repetitive and structured, making it possible to predict what information will appear next based on current sensory input.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that attentional selection can be so efficient because visual input is highly repetitive and structured, which makes it possible to predict what information will appear next based on the current sensory input (Friston, 2009; Kok et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Extracting regularities from the environment (statistical learning) occurs effortlessly across trials and operates largely outside conscious awareness.
source: Extracting these regularities from the environment, often called statistical learning (Chun and Jiang, 1999; Frost et al., 2015), occurs effortlessly across trials, operates largely outside the realm of conscious awareness, and is not contingent on explicit knowledge of the regularity (Gao and Theeuwes, 2022; Goujon et al., 2015; Turk-Browne et al., 2005; but see Vicente-Conesa et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Statistical learning plays a crucial role in attentional selection in addition to top-down and bottom-up control processes.
source: In addition to top-down and bottom-up control processes (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Desimone and Duncan, 1995; Theeuwes, 2010), statistical learning plays a crucial role in attentional selection (Awh et al., 2012; Failing and Theeuwes, 2018; Theeuwes et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: According to the tripartite model of attention, the interaction between top-down, bottom-up, and selection history jointly determines the weights in a spatial priority map.
source: According to the tripartite model of attention (Awh et al., 2012; Theeuwes, 2019; Theeuwes et al., 2022; Theeuwes, 2025), the interaction between top-down, bottom-up, and selection history, a category which encompasses statistical learning as well as other history-based effects, jointly determines the weights in a spatial priority map, which determines, in a winner-take-all fashion, which object is selected (Chelazzi et al., 2019; Zelinsky and Bisley, 2015).
evidence: This describes a theoretical model supported by citations.

claim: Observers can learn which location is most likely to contain the target.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that observers can learn which location is most likely to contain the target. Geng and Behrmann, 2005, showed that targets presented in high-probability locations (HPL) are detected faster than those in low-probability locations (LPL) (see also Ferrante et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Spatial enhancement occurs for the location with the highest likelihood of containing the target before display presentation.
source: Crucially, the probe task showed spatial enhancement for the location with the highest likelihood of containing the target. Based on these findings, it was argued that the amplification of weights within the spatial priority map, driven by statistical learning, takes place preemptively, before the actual display presentation, implying that priority was changed prior to the allocation of attention.
evidence: This is based on findings from Huang et al., 2022.

claim: A 'ping' technique can reveal hidden neural representations within networks of altered synaptic weights.
source: This technique pushes a wave of activity, often via presentation of a high-contrast stimulus, through the visual system to reveal hidden neural representations within networks of altered synaptic weights.
evidence: This describes the ping technique used in working memory research.

claim: Duncan et al., 2023, demonstrated reliable decoding of the high-probability target location in the evoked EEG signal when a visual ping occurred during the interval preceding the presentation of the search display.
source: Duncan et al., 2023, demonstrated that, following the acquisition of a learned priority for a specific spatial location, there was reliable decoding of the high-probability target location in the evoked EEG signal when a visual ping occurred during the interval preceding the presentation of the search display.
evidence: This is a specific finding from Duncan et al., 2023.

claim: Distractor interference is reduced when distractors appear at a high-probability distractor location compared to other locations.
source: Employing a modified version of the additional singleton paradigm, where the color singleton distractor appeared with a higher probability at a specific location relative to other locations, Wang and Theeuwes demonstrated that distractor interference was reduced when distractors appeared at this high-probability distractor location as compared to other locations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang and Theeuwes studies.

claim: Participants exhibited slower responses when the target was presented at the high-probability distractor location.
source: Furthermore, participants exhibited slower responses when the target was presented at this high-probability distractor location (Wang and Theeuwes, 2018b; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018a; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018c also see Ferrante et al., 2018; Goschy et al., 2014), suggesting that the spatial distractor imbalance resulted in learned suppression of the high-probability distractor location (Failing and Theeuwes, 2020; Feldmann-Wüstefeld et al., 2021; Ferrante et al., 2018; Goschy et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2021a; Sauter et al., 2021; Sauter et al., 2021; Allenmark et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022; van Moorselaar and Theeuwes, 2021b; van Moorselaar and Theeuwes, 2022; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018b; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Learned distractor suppression is not restricted to the spatial domain.
source: Such learned distractor suppression is not restricted to the spatial domain, as many studies have demonstrated that distractor interference can be attenuated, or even completely eliminated, through learning about probable distractor features (Gaspelin and Luck, 2018a; Stilwell and Gaspelin, 2021; Stilwell et al., 2022; Vatterott et al., 2018; Failing et al., 2019; Vatterott and Vecera, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to feature-based suppression studies.

claim: Suppression could potentially occur at three distinct time points: before the distractor appears, after distractor onset but before attentional capture, or after attentional capture has occurred.
source: As articulated by Liesefeld et al., 2024, suppression could potentially occur at three distinct time points: first, before the distractor appears, reflecting anticipatory preparation; second, after distractor onset but before attentional capture, indicating rapid early filtering; or third, after attentional capture has occurred.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework from Liesefeld et al., 2024.

claim: Responses were slowed when the probe appeared at the high-probability distractor location.
source: Across multiple studies it was found that responses were slowed when the probe appeared at the high-probability distractor location (Huang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2021b; Kong et al., 2020), even when the probe display was presented prior to the expected onset of the search display (Huang et al., 2023), leading to the conclusion that suppression operates prior to search display onset, and, thus, before the first shift of attention.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Chang et al., 2023, found that probe accuracy was higher at the high-probability distractor location compared to the low-probability location.
source: Contrary to a proactive account, Chang et al., 2023, found that while suppression occurred during the search task, as indicated by reaction times (RTs), probe accuracy was higher at the high-probability distractor location compared to the LPL (see Experiment 2 in Chang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a specific finding from Chang et al., 2023.

claim: The high-probability distractor location was initially selected for attentional processing before suppression occurred, supporting a reactive suppression mechanism.
source: This suggests that the HPL was initially selected for attentional processing before suppression occurred, supporting a reactive suppression mechanism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Chang et al., 2023 findings.

claim: Memory recall deviation was significantly larger at the test phase compared to the training phase.
source: Our findings revealed a significantly larger recall deviation at the test phase compared to the training phase (6.27°±0.95 vs 11.94°±3.55, t(23) = 5.67, p<0.001, d=2.52), indicating that the process of tracking the spatial memory cue was substantially disrupted by the concurrent secondary task in the test phase.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Overall memory recall performance in the test phase was high, indicating that observers were able to maintain a relatively precise memory representation outside the current focus of attention.
source: Note, that despite being disrupted by the search task, overall memory recall performance in the test phase was nevertheless high, indicating that observers were able to maintain a relatively precise memory representation outside the current focus of attention.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the memory performance data.

claim: Participants exhibited faster responses when the distractor appeared at the high-probability location compared to the low-probability location.
source: The planned paired t-test revealed that participants exhibited faster (t(23) = 10.14, p<0.001, d=0.43) and more accurate (t(23) = 5.19, p<0.001, d=0.71) responses when the distractor appeared at the HPL (MRT = 965 ms, MACC = 92.2%) compared to the LPL (MRT = 1017 ms, MACC = 89.5%), showing a clear effect of statistically learned distractor suppression and replicating previous findings (Ferrante et al., 2018; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Participants exhibited more accurate responses when the distractor appeared at the high-probability location compared to the low-probability location.
source: The planned paired t-test revealed that participants exhibited faster (t(23) = 10.14, p<0.001, d=0.43) and more accurate (t(23) = 5.19, p<0.001, d=0.71) responses when the distractor appeared at the HPL (MRT = 965 ms, MACC = 92.2%) compared to the LPL (MRT = 1017 ms, MACC = 89.5%), showing a clear effect of statistically learned distractor suppression and replicating previous findings (Ferrante et al., 2018; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: There was a substantial delay in participants' responses when the target was presented at the high-probability location as opposed to the low-probability location.
source: Further confirming the spatial component of suppression, a planned paired t-test on RTs for target location (collapsed across distractor-absent and distractor-present trials) demonstrated a substantial delay in participants' responses when the target was presented at the HPL (M=1018 ms), as opposed to the LPL (M=958 ms, t(23) = 5.45, p<0.001, d=0.48).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Learned suppression scaled with the relative distance to the high-probability location.
source: To further characterize whether the learned suppression scaled with the relative distance to the HPL, we assigned the low-probability trials into one of four distance groups depending on the relative distance between the distractor and the HPL.
evidence: This is tested through a distance-based analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: A significant main effect of distance was found in the analysis of reaction times.
source: A significant main effect was found in the analysis of RTs (F(2.22, 51.06)= 3.87, p = 0.023, ηp2 = 0.14).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the distance analysis.

claim: Responses in the dist-1 condition were faster than those in the dist-2 condition.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, responses in the dist-1 condition (Mdist_1=989 ms) were faster than those in the dist-2 condition (Mdist_2=1034 ms, t(23) = 3.96, p=0.003, d=0.36), and marginally faster than those in the dist-3 condition (Mdist_3=1024 ms, t(23) = 2.83, p=0.058, d=0.28) and dist-4 condition (Mdist_4=1033 ms, t(23) = 2.75, p=0.069, d=0.33).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mean accuracy analyses showed a main effect of distance.
source: Mean accuracy analyses mimicked these findings (see Figure 2D), showing a main effect of Distance (F(2.13, 49)= 4.20, p = 0.019, ηp2 = 0.15).
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Performance in the dist-1 condition was more accurate than in the dist-2 condition.
source: Performance in the dist-1 condition (Mdist_1=92.6%) was more accurate than in the dist-2 condition (Mdist_2=88.1%, t(23) = 4.24, p=0.002, d=0.86), and in the dist-3 condition (Mdist_3=88.7%, t(23) = 2.97, p=0.041, d=0.75), and marginally more accurate than in the dist-4 condition (Mdist_4=87.7%, t(23) = 2.87, p=0.052, d=0.73).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the distance analysis.

claim: Trials with repeated distractor locations were 41 ms faster compared to trials with non-repeated distractor locations.
source: Consistent with previous research, we found that trials with repeated distractor locations were 41 ms faster (t(23) = 6.32, p<0.001, d=0.33) and 2.1% more accurate (t(23) = 4.21, p<0.001, d=0.86) compared to trials with non-repeated distractor locations.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the intertrial effects analysis.

claim: Excluding trials with repeated distractor locations did not alter the main findings related to distractor regularity or the distance effect.
source: Importantly, excluding trials with repeated distractor locations did not alter the main findings related to distractor regularity or the distance effect, suggesting that intertrial effects alone cannot fully account for the learned suppression effects induced by spatial distractor imbalances.
evidence: This is a control analysis result.

claim: Both evoked and total alpha power generated reliable CTFs in response to memory display onset.
source: Consistent with previous work (Foster et al., 2016; Foster et al., 2017; van Moorselaar et al., 2018), both evoked and total alpha power generated reliable CTFs in response to memory display onset (p<0.05), with evoked power returning to baseline relatively early in the delayed period (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), whereas total alpha power enabled reliable CTF reconstruction throughout the entire delay period (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the localizer data analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The evoked CTFs were distinctly revived upon the presentation of the placeholder display.
source: Critically, as depicted in Figure 3B, the evoked CTFs were distinctly revived upon the presentation of the placeholder display (p<0.05).
evidence: This is a result from the localizer data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Individual CTF profiles following the memory cue onset were finely tuned to each of the eight spatial cue locations with comparable response strengths.
source: (C) illustrates that individual CTF profiles, following the memory cue onset, were finely tuned to each of the eight spatial cue locations with comparable response strengths.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Individual CTF profiles tuned to each of the eight spatial cue locations were revived by the placeholder to a similar extent.
source: (D) shows that individual CTF profiles tuned to each of the eight spatial cue locations were revived by the placeholder to a similar extent, although the effect was somewhat obscured in the fourth row of the panel.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The data from the training set did not exhibit a spatial bias from the outset.
source: These analyses confirm that the data from the training set did not exhibit a spatial bias from the outset and can thus serve as a neutral independent dataset to investigate how distractor learning in the test phase would, if at all, modulate attentional tuning across all display locations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the localizer data analysis.

claim: The averaged tuning profiles resulting from cross-session encoding mimicked the pattern of the localizer.
source: As depicted in Figure 4, the averaged tuning profiles resulting from this cross-session encoding procedure mimicked the pattern of the localizer, indicating that the training data could be used to successfully track the memoranda during the test phase with an intermediate search task.
evidence: This is a result from the cross-session encoding analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Total power no longer tracked the memorized position throughout the entire delay interval but instead returned to baseline prior to placeholder onset.
source: One main difference was observed on total power, such that it no longer tracked the memorized position throughout the entire delay interval but instead returned to baseline prior to placeholder onset (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the cross-session encoding analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Spatial information was revived by the placeholder, an effect that was selective to evoked power.
source: Critically, this information was again revived by the placeholder, an effect that was selective to evoked power (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from the cross-session encoding analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The prospect of a secondary task during the memory maintenance interval shifted the memory from an activity-driven into an activity-silent state.
source: Together, these findings are consistent with a model wherein the prospect of a secondary task during the memory maintenance interval shifted the memory from an activity-driven into an activity-silent state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-session encoding results.

claim: Upon placeholder onset, the instantiated neutral input probed the system's underlying activity-silent state, revealing its spatially tuned priority weights.
source: Upon placeholder onset, the instantiated neutral input probed the system's underlying activity-silent state, revealing its spatially tuned priority weights (analogous to the pinging procedure).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-session encoding results.

claim: The revival of the CTF by the placeholder display indicates that the hidden attentional priority map can still be reactivated despite the introduction of a secondary search task.
source: The revival of the CTF by the placeholder display indicates that the hidden attentional priority map, which tracks the location of the memory cue, can still be reactivated despite the introduction of a secondary search task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-session encoding results.

claim: During the memory encoding period and the maintenance period prior to placeholder onset, both the HPL-matched and LPL-matched CTFs are robust and highly overlap.
source: First, during the memory encoding period immediately following memory cue onset and the maintenance period prior to placeholder onset, both the HPL-matched and LPL-matched CTFs are robust (p<0.05) and highly overlap, indicating that, at this stage, the memory representation is unaffected by the spatial regularity of the distractor location.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Upon placeholder onset, reliable CTF reconstruction is observed in both HPL-matched and LPL-matched conditions, with the HPL-matched CTFs becoming numerically more pronounced than the LPL-matched CTFs.
source: Second, upon placeholder onset, reliable CTF reconstruction is observed in both conditions (p<0.05), with the HPL-matched CTFs becoming numerically more pronounced than the LPL-matched CTFs.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Memory cue locations overlapping with high-probability distractor locations were more strongly selected compared to those overlapping with low-probability locations.
source: Although this conditional difference was not statistically significant, the observed pattern suggests that memory cue locations overlapping with high-probability distractor locations were more strongly selected compared to those overlapping with LPL.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The resulting CTF profiles varied depending on their distances to the high-probability distractor location.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, in line with a spatial gradient, the resulting CTF profiles varied depending on their distances to the high-probability distractor location.
evidence: This is a result from the distance-based analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A cluster-based permutation test identified a reliable gradient centered around the high-probability location following placeholder onset.
source: A cluster-based permutation test conducted on the slopes of the regression model identified a reliable gradient (p<0.05) centered around the HPL following placeholder onset.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the distance-based analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The gradient reflected an increase of spatial selectivity centered at the high-probability distractor location rather than an attenuation.
source: Critically, this gradient reflected an increase of spatial selectivity centered at the high-probability distractor location rather than an attenuation, suggesting that immediately following placeholder onset the to-be-suppressed location was at least transiently attended before being suppressed during visual search in the subsequent display.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gradient analysis results.

claim: At the behavioral level, responses were faster when the distractor occurred at the high-probability location, but slower when the target occurred at this location.
source: At the behavioral level, responses were faster when the distractor occurred at the HPL, but slower when the target occurred at this location, indicative of generic spatial suppression, an effect that was characterized by a discernible spatial gradient centered at the high-probability distractor location.
evidence: This summarizes the behavioral findings in the Discussion.

claim: At the neural level, there was no evidence that spatial suppression attenuated processing at the high-probability distractor location in anticipation of a new search episode.
source: Yet, critically, at the neural level, there was no evidence that this spatial suppression attenuated processing at the high-probability distractor location in anticipation of a new search episode.
evidence: This summarizes the neural findings in the Discussion.

claim: The revival of the CTF profile within the alpha-band showed the largest tuning at the learned suppressed location.
source: Instead of a model that assumes that the HPL was proactively suppressed, the revival of the CTF profile within the alpha-band showed the largest tuning at the learned suppressed location.
evidence: This summarizes the key neural finding in the Discussion.

claim: The modulation of the memory-tuned CTF profile was characterized by a spatial gradient that was centered over the high-probability location.
source: Moreover, the modulation of the memory-tuned CTF profile was characterized by a spatial gradient that was centered over the HPL.
evidence: This summarizes the gradient finding in the Discussion.

claim: Suppression is engaged following the initial selection of a location, indicating a tendency toward a reactive suppression mechanism.
source: These findings suggest that suppression is engaged following the initial selection of a location, indicating a tendency toward a reactive suppression mechanism within the specific context of our study.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: Suppression may occur after attentional enhancement rather than being proactively implemented.
source: This implies that suppression may occur after attentional enhancement rather than being proactively implemented.
evidence: This is an implication of the main conclusion.

claim: Studies investigating the preparatory bias in response to distractor regularities largely failed to find evidence in support of active preparatory inhibition as indexed via increased alpha power contralateral to the high-probability distractor location.
source: Studies investigating the preparatory bias in response to distractor regularities largely examined topographical modulations of alpha power, given its functional link to reduced cortical excitability. These studies, however, failed to find evidence in support of active preparatory inhibition as indexed via increased alpha power contralateral to the high-probability distractor location (van Moorselaar et al., 2021a; van Moorselaar et al., 2020a; van Moorselaar and Slagter, 2019; but see Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The absence of anticipatory tuning toward the to-be-suppressed location has given rise to the idea that distractor learning operates by changing synaptic efficiency within these regions.
source: This absence of anticipatory tuning toward the to-be-suppressed location has given rise to the idea that distractor learning operates by changing synaptic efficiency within these regions (van Moorselaar and Slagter, 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van Moorselaar and Slagter, 2020b.

claim: A recent study using rapid invisible frequency tagging demonstrated reduced neural excitability at the high-probability distractor location in the absence of any alpha-band modulations.
source: Consistent with this, a recent study using rapid invisible frequency tagging demonstrated reduced neural excitability at the high-probability distractor location in the absence of any alpha-band modulations (Ferrante et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ferrante et al., 2023.

claim: The revived CTFs were characterized by a spatial gradient centered over the high-probability location, with tuning being most pronounced at the to-be-suppressed location.
source: Interestingly, rather than being suppressed, the revived CTFs were characterized by a spatial gradient centered over the HPL, with tuning being most pronounced at the to-be-suppressed location.
evidence: This is a key finding from the study.

claim: The putative priority map, initially tuned by maintaining a spatial location in working memory, was reconfigured by statistical regularities across search displays to align with the imminent search.
source: Together, this suggests that the putative priority map, initially tuned by maintaining a spatial location in WM, was reconfigured by statistical regularities across search displays to align with the imminent search.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: If one assumes that the evoked response elicited by placeholder displays ping the landscape of the priority map, the observed gradient clearly argues against proactive suppression.
source: If one assumes that the evoked response elicited by placeholder displays ping the landscape of this priority map (Duncan et al., 2023), the observed gradient in our study clearly argues against proactive suppression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of the pinging technique.

claim: A recent behavioral study observed a similar pattern of results showing initial enhancement at the high-probability distractor location before suppression.
source: Although this result is based on an exploratory analysis and should therefore be interpreted with caution, it is noteworthy that a recent behavioral study observed a similar pattern of results (Chang et al., 2023). In a modified version of the capture-probe paradigm, where the probe display onset was not preceded by a placeholder display, participants discriminated the orientation of a tilted bar presented at one of the search locations, revealing initial enhancement at the high-probability distractor location before suppression.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chang et al., 2023.

claim: Memory performance (recall) did not vary as a function of the cue's distance from the high-probability location.
source: Memory performance (recall) did not vary as a function of the cue's distance from the HPL (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1), whereas the revived CTFs did, indicating that these changes likely reflect contributions from both tasks.
evidence: This is a result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Distractor learning typically occurs without conscious awareness.
source: Additionally, distractor learning typically occurs without conscious awareness (Gao and Theeuwes, 2022; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The current results clearly argue against a model wherein statistical learning operates by downregulating weights at the to-be-suppressed location.
source: Irrespective however, the current results clearly argue against a model wherein statistical learning operates by downregulating weights at the to-be-suppressed location.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.

claim: Proactive and reactive suppression processes may not be mutually exclusive and may often contribute concurrently to observed attentional effects.
source: While many studies, including the current one, have attempted to dissociate between proactive and reactive suppression mechanisms, it is plausible that these processes are not mutually exclusive and may often contribute concurrently to observed attentional effects.
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration in the Discussion.

claim: A study by Wang et al., 2019, showed that fewer saccades landed at the suppressed location than any other location, consistent with less proactive oculomotor activity at the suppressed location.
source: A study by Wang et al., 2019, showed that fewer saccades landed at the suppressed location than any other location, consistent with the notion that there was less proactive oculomotor activity at the suppressed location resulting in fewer saccades to that location.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: There was evidence for faster disengagement from the high-probability distractor location than the low-probability distractor location, suggesting a reactive mechanism.
source: Critically however, there was also evidence for faster disengagement from the high-probability distractor location than the low-probability distractor location, suggesting the operation of a reactive mechanism where suppression is followed by rapid oculomotor disengagement (Sauter et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sauter et al., 2021.

claim: Visual pings can effectively unveil spatial memories hidden from the ongoing EEG signal.
source: A novel aspect of the current study is that visual pings, here in the shape of a neutral placeholder display, can effectively unveil spatial memories hidden from the ongoing EEG signal.
evidence: This is a key methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The otherwise invisible attentional priority map induced by a spatial imbalance of target probability across trials could be revealed by the 'pinging' technique in conjunction with multivariate pattern analysis and EEG.
source: Recently, we demonstrated that the otherwise, invisible attentional priority map induced by a spatial imbalance of target probability across trials could also be revealed by the 'pinging' technique in conjunction with multivariate pattern analysis and EEG (Duncan et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Duncan et al., 2023.

claim: Early ERP components are enhanced in response to visual stimulation at memorized locations.
source: However, while it is well established that early ERP components are enhanced in response to visual stimulation at memorized locations (Awh et al., 2000), to date the pinging technique has exclusively been used to reveal feature-specific information within working memory (Wolff et al., 2015; Wolff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is an ongoing debate surrounding the precise mechanisms underlying the ping effect, particularly whether it reactivates latent networks or merely amplifies existing, yet below-threshold representations within ongoing neural activity.
source: Despite initial enthusiasm within this field, there is an ongoing debate surrounding the precise mechanisms underlying the ping effect, particularly whether it reactivates latent networks or merely amplifies existing, yet below-threshold representations within ongoing neural activity (Barbosa et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Barbosa et al., 2021.

claim: Skepticism arises from demonstrations that measurable neural activity often underlies working memory maintenance.
source: Additionally, skepticism arises from demonstrations that measurable neural activity often underlies working memory maintenance (Schneegans and Bays, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schneegans and Bays, 2017.

claim: During the training phase, CTFs continuously tracked the position of the spatial memory cue.
source: During the training phase, where the memory task was the only task at hand, CTFs continuously tracked the position of the spatial memory cue.
evidence: This is a result from the study.

claim: The same reconstruction returned to baseline when the model was applied to the test session that incorporated a search task during the maintenance interval.
source: However, the same reconstruction returned to baseline when the model was applied to the test session that incorporated a search task during the maintenance interval.
evidence: This is a result from the study.

claim: Under dual-task conditions, memories might be strategically offloaded to a mechanism relying on weak neural activity or one not dependent on sustained neural firing at all.
source: This suggests the possibility that under dual-task conditions memories might be strategically offloaded to a mechanism relying on weak neural activity or even one not dependent on sustained neural firing at all, such as an activity-silent representation facilitated by synaptic plasticity or long-term memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The content of a hidden spatial representation can be revived by flooding the visual system with sensory input.
source: Regardless of the precise underlying mechanism, our results demonstrate in a compelling way that the content of a hidden spatial representation can be revived by flooding the visual system with sensory input.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.
